guide.feature.analog-movement.32: Vanilla Minecraft only sees WASD as on/off, so stick-to-keys walking is limited to eight directions at full speed. With Analog Movement, Control Flex feeds a continuous 360° vector: any angle, and a light push walks slowly.
guide.feature.analog-movement.37: Direction and magnitude used as-is — the console feel
guide.feature.analog-movement.38: Singleplayer, LAN, and servers that tolerate smooth movement
guide.feature.analog-movement.40: Stick snapped to eight directions at full speed, which looks like keyboard input to a server
guide.feature.analog-movement.45: Public servers and Realms → keyboard-like 8-way, so analog walk is less likely to look like abnormal input to server-side anti-cheat
guide.feature.analog-movement.47: Control Flex Settings → Other → Analog Movement: master switch plus policy.
guide.feature.analog-movement.48: Server whitelist: if a specific remote server should still get Analog Smooth, add it (host:port or Realm name) on the same page.
guide.feature.analog-movement.49: Turning the master switch off restores digital WASD bindings; the policy then does nothing.
guide.feature.analog-movement.51: Two more knobs live on the Calibration page: stick deadzones (one value per stick, saved per controller) and the movement response curve. If a light push does nothing or drifts, run auto calibration first, then fine-tune the deadzone, and only then adjust the response curve.
guide.feature.analog-movement.52: Looking keyboard-like on a server only changes the shape of the movement vector; every action key you press behaves exactly the same.
guide.feature.analog-movement.53: Related: Camera & Aim (the look curve also lives under Calibration) and Settings & Controls (calibration steps).
guide.feature.camera.32: The right stick drives the camera, updating yaw and pitch at render frame rate for smoothness. Three modes cover everything from vanilla play to combat mods.
guide.feature.camera.37: Stick moves the camera directly; the most responsive
guide.feature.camera.39: Turns with smoothing, closer to a console feel
guide.feature.camera.40: Everyday play where a follow-through feel is wanted
guide.feature.camera.41: Look is routed through the mouse pipeline (MouseHandler), so mods that intercept the mouse still see crosshair movement
guide.feature.camera.42: Combat mods with custom aiming such as Epic Fight (on by default for new installs)
guide.feature.camera.45: Response curve: a quadratic curve that gives finer control at small deflections, tuned in Camera Settings; it belongs to the same Calibration family as stick deadzones.
guide.feature.camera.46: Y-axis invert: optional, toggled in Camera Settings.
guide.feature.camera.47: Frame-rate independent: look uses the frame delta, so it neither speeds up at high refresh rates nor lags at low ones.
guide.feature.camera.49: Zoom slowdown (sensitivity compensation while scoping) only applies in Simulate Mouse mode, matching what mods expect from the mouse pipeline. Zoom itself is a bindable action (unbound in the Basic template).
guide.feature.camera.51: Simulate Mouse cannot drive the OS cursor in a background window, so it automatically falls back to Direct Turn there. For couch co-op, use Direct Turn or Smooth Turn (see Split-Screen Co-op).
guide.feature.camera.52: Related: Cursor & GUI (aiming inside menus) and Analog Movement (movement response curves).
guide.feature.combo-keys.32: When one button is not enough, press several: bind a chord such as LB + Back or LT + A to a single action. Rare-but-important actions no longer need a dedicated face button.
guide.feature.combo-keys.34: Select the target row in Key Mapping to start capture.
guide.feature.combo-keys.35: Press the first button, then add the rest within 500 ms; the UI shows the full chord as it builds.
guide.feature.combo-keys.36: Once complete, all buttons must be down together for the action to fire — pressing one of them alone still performs its own binding.
guide.feature.combo-keys.37: ESC cancels capture; right-click a row to clear, reset, or move it to another layer.
guide.feature.combo-keys.38: The capture window is fixed at 500 ms; it does not follow the Tap threshold.
guide.feature.combo-keys.40: Upgrade rule: when a larger chord activates (say A+B+Y), any active smaller chord whose buttons are a proper subset of it (A+B) is destroyed. Behavior stays predictable.
guide.feature.combo-keys.41: Button sharing (reference counting): one physical button can take part in several chords; the engine tracks references so they do not interfere.
guide.feature.combo-keys.42: Every trigger mode works: chords support the same ten modes as single-key bindings, including all the Double variants.
guide.feature.combo-keys.47: Second function on a common key
guide.feature.combo-keys.48: Basic template: R-stick click + D-Pad ↓ = drop stack
guide.feature.combo-keys.49: Plain “drop” already has a button; the rarer stack-drop rides on a chord
guide.feature.combo-keys.51: Direction chords on the attack trigger are easy to remember as a pair
guide.feature.combo-keys.53: Hold a layer switch, then press a chord on that layer
guide.feature.combo-keys.54: Extends layouts further without spending Main-layer slots
guide.feature.combo-keys.56: A chord requires every button to be held at once; if one of them is heavily used as a Hold binding (say LT for “use”), including it makes accidental chords more likely — choose deliberately.
guide.feature.combo-keys.57: Chords respect the global Tap / Long Press thresholds too (Double modes use the Tap threshold as their gap).
guide.feature.combo-keys.58: In template JSON a chord joins button names with +: "drop_stack": "rightStickClick+dpadDown|PRESS".
guide.feature.combo-keys.59: Related: Seven Layers (each layer has its own chord space) and Trigger Modes (the mode set chords can use).
guide.feature.cursor.32: Once a chest or inventory is open, a pad has to point, click, and drag like a mouse. The Screen layer covers this with three mechanisms: a virtual cursor, slot snapping, and D-Pad slot jumps.
guide.feature.cursor.34: How it moves: the left stick's raw axis values are routed through Minecraft's mouse event pipeline — a separate mechanism from the direction bindings (cursor_navi_*).
guide.feature.cursor.35: Cursor speed: 2–20 pixels per tick, tuned in Cursor Settings.
guide.feature.cursor.36: Cursor style: the system cursor, a Bedrock-style set, or a hand style (textures ship with the cursor style packs).
guide.feature.cursor.38: On by default, switchable in Cursor Settings.
guide.feature.cursor.39: When the stick stops, the cursor snaps to the nearest container slot; the snap distance is adjustable from 1–80 pixels.
guide.feature.cursor.40: Only active while holding an item — an empty hand moves the cursor freely without sticking.
guide.feature.cursor.41: Hover slowdown: with snapping on, the cursor slows while hovering a slot for precise selection.
guide.feature.cursor.43: When precision is not needed, the D-Pad jumps between slots directly. It uses cone-shaped targeting, so long horizontal rows and irregular grids (custom containers) still jump reliably. Slot jumps coexist with the virtual cursor — the left stick takes over free movement at any time.
guide.feature.cursor.60: All of these live on the Screen layer of Key Mapping and can be changed row by row; LB/RB tab switching also works for creative tabs, recipe-book pages, and the guide list.
guide.feature.cursor.61: Beyond: Screens That Only Read Physical Keys
guide.feature.cursor.62: Some mod screens ignore the virtual cursor and only react to keyboard/mouse events — use Virtual Keyboard & Mouse to inject real keys there (e.g. map B to physical Esc). To customize stick behavior per screen (Independent / Radial Path / Virtual Mouse), add a Screen rule in Mod Adaptation.
guide.feature.guide-hud.32: No need to alt-tab to a document: Control Flex brings the reference into the game. Context HUD tips appear for the current action, held item, open screen, or controller button, and the guide list gathers everything available.
guide.feature.guide-hud.34: Guide entries can be marked for HUD display: those tips appear on screen in context — the movement and interaction basics when you first join, tips for a specific held item, or the key hints for a screen you just opened. Entries reference Control Flex actions directly, so your own rebinds are reflected in the tips.
guide.feature.guide-hud.36: Press the Guide button to open the list (open_guide, bound to Guide in the Basic template); LB / RB switch tabs inside.
guide.feature.guide-hud.37: The list is organized by category; each guide has a trigger (such as “first join”) plus entries made of an action, a label, and a display mode.
guide.feature.guide-hud.39: Glyphs in the tips follow the connected controller: Xbox, PlayStation, and Switch layouts each have their own mappings, and the Nintendo layout handles the A/B swap — so the same tip shows the right icons on a DualSense and an Xbox pad alike.
guide.feature.guide-hud.41: Guide JSON lives in config/controlflex/guides/ (layered: default/ packaged, mods/ installed by bridge mods, user/ your edits); the packaged defaults are copied out on first run. Structure (excerpt):
guide.feature.guide-hud.43: Pack authors: ship a guide describing your pack's controller layout so new players see it the moment they join.
guide.feature.guide-hud.44: Bridge mods: install guide assets alongside compat configs (onInstallGuideAssets, see Setup & lifecycle) to add tips for key actions.
guide.feature.guide-hud.45: Related: Settings & Controls (the key-detection panel for debugging missing tips) and the API Reference (reloadGuides() and IControllerCapabilities).
guide.feature.layers.32: A standard pad has roughly a dozen inputs; a modpack can expose hundreds of actions. The seven-layer model lets one physical button mean different things per context — it is the foundation everything else builds on.
guide.feature.layers.38: Movement, look, combat, hotbar, and everyday mod actions
guide.feature.layers.39: While the matching layer switch is held
guide.feature.layers.40: Four modifier planes, each with a full binding table; releasing the switch returns to Main
guide.feature.layers.41: Whenever a screen is open (inventory, chests, mod UIs, settings)
guide.feature.layers.42: Confirm, back, tab switching, scrolling, slot navigation, container helpers; opening a menu never fights your gameplay bindings
guide.feature.layers.43: Interactive HUDs (spell wheels, third-party radial menus, photo HUDs)
guide.feature.layers.44: Explicit bindings, no Main inheritance: unconfigured actions stay silent so a HUD cannot misfire combat keys
guide.feature.layers.46: Shift layers are four independent binding planes. Four rules explain the whole feature:
guide.feature.layers.47: Movement and look keys default to Main's values (pre-filled when the template is created); everything else defaults to unbound — the layers are fully explicit.
guide.feature.layers.48: Editing Main later does not change Shift layers, and vice versa. Each layer owns its table.
guide.feature.layers.49: Layer switches are fixed to HOLD (the layer_shift1–4 rows on Main cannot use another mode).
guide.feature.layers.50: Each Shift layer auto-derives a “return to Main” binding with RELEASE mode — releasing the switch returns you, no manual setup.
guide.feature.layers.51: Common misconception: Shift layers do not inherit Main at runtime — an empty slot is simply unbound. Templates merely pre-fill movement and look with Main's values so you have a sensible starting point.
guide.feature.layers.53: Whenever any screen is open, input switches to the Screen layer. Defaults fall into four groups:
guide.feature.layers.54: Cursor: the left stick drives the virtual cursor (direction bindings can navigate it too; the two are separate rows).
guide.feature.layers.55: Slots: D-Pad jumps between slots, A selects, Y quick-moves (shift-click), X takes half.
guide.feature.layers.56: Navigation: A confirm, B back/close, LB/RB switch pages (creative tabs, recipe-book pages, the guide list).
guide.feature.layers.57: Scrolling: right stick up/down emulates the wheel; left/right taps cycle options.
guide.feature.layers.58: The Screen layer can also inject physical keys such as the scroll wheel (see Virtual Keyboard & Mouse); cursor details live in Cursor & GUI.
guide.feature.layers.60: The Overlay layer covers interactive HUDs that are neither a full screen nor plain gameplay — spell wheels, third-party radial menus, photo/attachment HUDs. Its defaults follow the in-game feel (move, look, jump, attack, use, scroll) with B as back. Two things matter:
guide.feature.layers.61: No Main inheritance: unconfigured actions stay silent during an overlay, so a HUD cannot misfire combat keys. Layer switches are suppressed while an overlay is open.
guide.feature.layers.62: The HUD must be declared: add an Overlay rule for it in Mod Adaptation, or use the Control Flex API's IInteractiveContextRegistrar from a bridge mod (see the API Reference). Keys that must stay held across an overlay can be phase-locked until you unlock them.
guide.feature.layers.64: Key Mapping shows and edits bindings per layer: switch the layer tab, or edit any layer's rows.
guide.feature.layers.65: Which layers an action appears on is configured per action in its detail page. Switching templates resets layer placement to template defaults; “reset to template defaults” does not change layer placement.
guide.feature.layers.66: Click the controller column to capture input; ESC cancels; right-click a row to clear, reset, or change its layer.
guide.feature.layers.70: Unbound — assign them yourself when needed (paddles are a good fit)
guide.feature.layers.73: To go beyond layers: combo keys add density to a single layer, and radial menus keep frequent actions on a wheel.
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.32: Control Flex is built for modpacks: most mods work out of the box. When one sits on the wrong layer or its screen misbehaves, the adaptation chain solves it in escalating steps — in-game center → community repo → compat JSON → bridge mod.
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.34: At startup Control Flex scans Minecraft's KeyMapping registry and registers every non-vanilla binding as a bindable action, then reconciles again when you open settings — so nothing gets missed. Library mods (the Fabric API and Kotlin language-support families) are exempted and never clutter the lists.
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.36: Open Control Flex Settings → Mod Adaptation: every installed mod is listed with name, icon, and version. Each mod has three tabs:
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.37: Key Bindings: the mod's discovered actions, assigned to layers (Main / Screen / Overlay) and bound straight to gamepad buttons.
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.38: Screen Adaptation: stick mode, layer mapping, and cursor rules while that mod's GUI is open.
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.39: Overlay Adaptation: the same, for interactive HUDs (spell wheels, photo HUDs, and similar).
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.40: Adding a rule: open the target GUI or HUD once in-game so Control Flex records it, then use + Add Screen/Overlay Adaptation in the mod's page and pick it from the recent-pages list (up to 50). Entries that could not be matched to a mod can be scanned automatically.
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.45: Stick directions act as actions bound on Layer Mapping
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.46: Both sticks on Overlay; the right stick on Screen
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.47: Stick traces a path or angle — spell wheels and ring menus
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.49: Stick moves a cursor inside that UI
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.51: With no rule: Screen uses Virtual Mouse on the left stick and Independent on the right; Overlay keeps both sticks Independent. Cursor style offers system / Bedrock / hand; Virtual Mouse has a speed setting, and Radial Path has threshold, radius, angle bias, and whether the last angle is restored.
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.53: The official community source is ControlFlexMC/cfx-compat-configs. From Mod Adaptation: Sync Configs → browse variants → preview Bindings / Screen / Overlay → Apply (existing user files are backed up first). Extra sources can be added, and local JSON can be imported or exported from a mod's page.
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.55: All edits are copy-on-write: packaged and community files stay read-only and your changes land in config/controlflex/compat/user/. A mod's Reset Config restores its packaged or applied community default. Packaged rules sit behind every mod — the JAR ships three (JEI, Epic Fight, Nightfall), and each only activates when its target mod is actually loaded.
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.56: Step Four: If It Still Misbehaves
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.57: Check Key Mapping — is the action on the right layer?
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.58: Add a Screen/Overlay rule, or apply a community config.
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.60: Bypasses KeyMapping entirely → hand-write or share compat JSON, or write a bridge mod.
guide.feature.mod-adaptation.61: For compat JSON fields, layer priority, and pack distribution, see Mod Compatibility; for bridge-mod development, see Bridge Mods.
guide.feature.radial-menus.32: Up to five independent wheels, each with as many as eight slots around the stick: open a wheel, aim with the stick, confirm with A. Food, torches, /home — frequent actions that do not deserve a dedicated face button belong on a wheel.
guide.feature.radial-menus.38: Fires a vanilla or mod KeyMapping
guide.feature.radial-menus.43: Switches to the hotbar slot and uses it
guide.feature.radial-menus.46: Opening follows the menu's binding: Press taps to open (release does not close it), Hold keeps it open while held and closes on release.
guide.feature.radial-menus.47: Selection stick: left, right, or both (both by default).
guide.feature.radial-menus.48: Menus are assigned to layers: by default Menu 1 lives on Main and Menus 2–5 on Shift 1–4 — Shift layers serve as wheel entry points as well as binding planes.
guide.feature.radial-menus.50: Icon modes: auto (inferred from the slot's content, e.g. item icons), random, default, item ID, or a custom texture path.
guide.feature.radial-menus.51: The in-game editor lets you pick icons, reorder slots, and set the trigger mode per menu.
guide.feature.radial-menus.53: Wheel layouts persist in config/controlflex/radial_menu/radial_menus.json with icons alongside. Packs can ship this file so players start with working wheels. Structure (excerpt):
guide.feature.radial-menus.62: All slots ship empty — a wheel is a container you (or a pack author) fill. The same Back button opens five different wheels because each menu belongs to a different layer.
guide.feature.radial-menus.63: Related: Seven Layers (wheels hang off layers) and Configuration (shipping wheel layouts in a pack).
guide.feature.rumble.32: Minecraft events translated into controller vibration: seven waveforms, configured per event type, with light / medium / heavy intensity bands — taking a hit and scoring a kill can feel completely different.
guide.feature.rumble.39: A short jolt, good for light hits
guide.feature.rumble.43: Ramps up from light to strong
guide.feature.rumble.45: Continuous buzz for big events like explosions
guide.feature.rumble.49: A lub-dub rhythm, good for tension or low-health moments
guide.feature.rumble.51: Damage types: fall, fire, drown, mob, player, explosion, other — each picks its own waveform (including “none”).
guide.feature.rumble.52: Entity kills: kills can have their own feedback.
guide.feature.rumble.53: Intensity bands: global light / medium / heavy thresholds, so the same damage type can hit differently depending on severity.
guide.feature.rumble.54: Master switch: turn everything off in one place.
guide.feature.rumble.56: Open Control Flex Settings → Rumble and confirm the current pad reports rumble support (pads without it simply do nothing here).
guide.feature.rumble.57: Use the built-in intensity tests to feel light / medium / heavy, then set thresholds.
guide.feature.rumble.58: Pick waveforms per type: a pulse for falls, a sustained buzz for explosions, and a distinct feel for player damage.
guide.feature.rumble.59: In multiplayer your rumble follows your own settings; the events that drive it come from the game itself, so singleplayer and server play behave the same.
guide.feature.rumble.60: Related: Mod Adaptation (bringing mod events into Control Flex actions) and the API Reference (IControllerCapabilities.hasRumble() for bridge mods).
guide.feature.splitscreen.32: Java Edition does not render two players in one window, so couch co-op means two clients on one PC joined over Open to LAN, each with its own controller. Control Flex supports that setup in two specific ways: controller ownership and unfocused windows that keep playing.
guide.feature.splitscreen.34: Two or more Minecraft accounts — offline accounts are fine. Two different offline usernames in the same launcher are enough; you do not need a second Microsoft account.
guide.feature.splitscreen.35: Two gamepads, or one gamepad plus keyboard and mouse.
guide.feature.splitscreen.36: A launcher that can run two instances at once (see below).
guide.feature.splitscreen.37: Control Flex installed in each instance that uses a gamepad.
guide.feature.splitscreen.38: Optional: Splitscreen Support (window tiling only, no input handling).
guide.feature.splitscreen.40: Create one launcher instance per account; keep both windowed (not fullscreen).
guide.feature.splitscreen.41: Install the mods: Control Flex in the gamepad instances, optionally Splitscreen Support too.
guide.feature.splitscreen.42: Launch both. Two pads: pick a different controller in each game's Gamepad Selection. Pad + keyboard: assign the pad in the gamepad instance only.
guide.feature.splitscreen.43: Press F3+P in each window to disable Pause on Lost Focus (or change it in video options) — the unfocused window must keep running; the pause screen also shows a hint.
guide.feature.splitscreen.44: With Splitscreen Support, press F11 to cycle half- and quarter-screen layouts; the last position is remembered.
guide.feature.splitscreen.45: Host on one instance (Open to LAN); join from the others from the multiplayer list, or via localhost plus the port shown.
guide.feature.splitscreen.47: Use Direct Turn or Smooth Turn in background windows.
guide.feature.splitscreen.48: Simulate Mouse cannot drive the OS cursor in a background window and falls back to Direct Turn automatically — use Direct or Smooth everywhere to avoid the switch.
guide.feature.splitscreen.49: “Input stealing” is the classic two-pad problem: SDL3 reports devices honestly, but both clients might pick the same one. Just assign different devices in Gamepad Selection. When a pad disconnects, Control Flex auto-selects the first available one, so keep each player on their own device.
guide.feature.splitscreen.50: Related: Camera & Aim (look mode details) and Seven Layers (each player keeps their own template and config).
guide.feature.splitscreen.56: What matters is real instance isolation — one folder of mods/, config/ and saves per instance. These launchers give you that out of the box, so two clients can run side by side without fighting over the same files.
guide.feature.splitscreen.60: Windows · macOS · Linux — open-source MultiMC fork with true instance isolation: each instance has its own mods/, config/, saves and Java version. Offline accounts are added right on the Accounts page.
guide.feature.splitscreen.61: Windows · macOS · Linux — keeps an explicit instance list with one folder each, and can import CurseForge / Modrinth packs.
guide.feature.splitscreen.62: Windows · macOS · Linux — its version isolation keeps one game directory per version, offline login is supported, and the interface is available in Chinese.
guide.feature.splitscreen.63: Windows · macOS — instances are kept apart from each other; Linux support is still experimental.
guide.feature.splitscreen.64: Two things about offline accounts: give each instance a different username — that name is the in-game player name, and duplicates collide on the LAN — and Open to LAN does not verify accounts, so offline clients join directly. Only a dedicated server needs online-mode=false in server.properties.
guide.feature.trigger-modes.32: Every binding pairs which button with how it fires. Control Flex offers ten trigger modes, so one button can tap, hold, latch, and double-press for different actions.
guide.feature.trigger-modes.42: Movement, look, sustained use, layer switches
guide.feature.trigger-modes.43: Once, on release after a short press; if held past the threshold, nothing fires on release
guide.feature.trigger-modes.44: Quick actions that must not fire on a hold
guide.feature.trigger-modes.45: Once, after being held past the long-press threshold
guide.feature.trigger-modes.46: A second function on the same button (e.g. pause menu)
guide.feature.trigger-modes.47: First press activates and holds, second press releases; independent of button hold (RELEASE events are ignored)
guide.feature.trigger-modes.48: Persistent states: sprint, walk mode, POV
guide.feature.trigger-modes.49: A second press inside the tap window fires once immediately on down (not latched)
guide.feature.trigger-modes.50: An extra one-shot alongside Hold / Press
guide.feature.trigger-modes.51: Two short presses; fires once on the second release
guide.feature.trigger-modes.52: Confirm-style actions that must not steal the first tap
guide.feature.trigger-modes.53: Short press, then press-and-hold inside the tap window; stays active until release
guide.feature.trigger-modes.54: Tap-then-hold for deliberate triggers that resist misfires
guide.feature.trigger-modes.55: Same latch as Toggle; flips on the second short-press release
guide.feature.trigger-modes.56: A latch sharing one button with its Hold variant (Basic does this for sneak)
guide.feature.trigger-modes.58: Tap and Long Press thresholds are global, 100–2000 ms, configured in Other Settings. They apply to every binding and template.
guide.feature.trigger-modes.59: The Tap threshold doubles as the gap limit for every Double mode: Double Press / Tap / Hold / Toggle all use it as the maximum interval between the two presses.
guide.feature.trigger-modes.60: Defaults: Tap 500 ms, Long Press 1000 ms (from the Basic template).
guide.feature.trigger-modes.62: In Key Mapping, the Mode column cycles through the common modes (Press / Hold / Tap / Long Press).
guide.feature.trigger-modes.63: Templates and compat JSON support all ten, written as button|MODE — for example buttonA|HOLD or rightStickClick|DOUBLE_TOGGLE. Mode tokens: PRESS / RELEASE / HOLD / TAP / LONG_PRESS / TOGGLE / DOUBLE_PRESS / DOUBLE_TAP / DOUBLE_HOLD / DOUBLE_TOGGLE.
guide.feature.trigger-modes.64: Some actions restrict their mode: layer switches are fixed to HOLD, Shift-layer return-to-Main to RELEASE, and radial-menu opens support PRESS and HOLD.
guide.feature.trigger-modes.70: Hold to sneak, double-tap to latch sneak (Basic default)
guide.feature.trigger-modes.71: Long press opens the pause menu; short presses do nothing
guide.feature.trigger-modes.72: Tap to change perspective; an accidental hold does nothing
guide.feature.trigger-modes.73: To combine buttons into one action, see Combo Keys; to bake toggles into a template, see Configuration.
guide.feature.virtual-kbm.32: Some mods never register a KeyMapping — they only watch the physical keyboard or mouse. Virtual KBM lets the gamepad inject real key events (Shift, Escape, Page Up/Down, mouse buttons, the scroll wheel) without turning them into Control Flex actions first.
guide.feature.virtual-kbm.34: In Key Mapping, find the Virtual KBM section and add an entry: press the keyboard/mouse key you want to inject (e.g. Escape or the wheel).
guide.feature.virtual-kbm.35: Then bind a controller combo to it on any layer (a single button or a chord) and enable that layer.
guide.feature.virtual-kbm.36: Entries enable per layer: the same physical key can fire only on Main, only in GUI, or both — the shipped defaults are written that way (see the table below).
guide.feature.virtual-kbm.38: Scroll wheel: a tap scrolls one notch; holding repeats — one notch per 100 ms by default, configurable.
guide.feature.virtual-kbm.39: GUI back is a real Esc: B in a screen sends a physical Esc, identical to clicking Esc with a mouse — mod screens that reject gamepad input still close properly.
guide.feature.virtual-kbm.40: Never types into chat: injected keys do not enter chat or text fields.
guide.feature.virtual-kbm.41: Careful: an injected key can fire alongside an existing action binding (e.g. LT both runs a Control Flex action and injects Left Shift). Watch for overlaps and put them on different layers when needed.
guide.feature.virtual-kbm.48: Bound to LT on the GUI layer (quick move / stacking)
guide.feature.virtual-kbm.52: Work down this list: (1) the mod's keys are in KeyMapping → just use them (auto-discovery); (2) wrong layer or stick behavior → add a rule in Mod Adaptation; (3) only physical keys are read → Virtual KBM; (4) the mod bypasses KeyMapping entirely → it needs a bridge mod (see the bridge mod docs).
guide.feature.virtual-kbm.53: Related: Cursor & GUI and Mod Compatibility (the full troubleshooting checklist).

guide.platforms.19: Control Flex reads controllers through libgamepadjni + SDL3. On desktop, both the native library and SDL3 ship inside the JAR, so it works out of the box; on Android, SDL3 must come from the launcher APK, which is why behaviour varies a little between launchers.
guide.platforms.32: Provided by the launcher APK; never bundled
guide.platforms.35: Detection reads os.version only: a value starting with Android- means Android, everything else is treated as desktop. os.name (Android launchers also report Linux) is written to diagnostic logs and never used for detection.
guide.platforms.37: No SDL3, driver, or extra runtime to install — the mod always uses the SDL3 packaged in the JAR, so it neither conflicts with a system SDL nor searches system paths.
guide.platforms.38: Both Windows x86_64 and ARM64 ship native binaries (gamepadjni.dll + SDL3.dll).
guide.platforms.39: macOS ships both Intel and Apple Silicon libgamepadjni.dylib builds, so it works with or without Rosetta.
guide.platforms.40: Linux ships x86_64 and aarch64 libgamepadjni.so builds, covering aarch64 devices such as Steam Deck.
guide.platforms.41: Hotplug, multi-controller detection, and per-controller identity (name / type / serial) behave the same across the three desktop platforms.
guide.platforms.43: On Android, Minecraft: Java Edition runs on a JVM provided by a launcher, so the controller path is split in two: SDL3 comes from the launcher APK (the launcher already installed the SDL glue on the ART side), while libgamepadjni.so ships with the mod and is extracted per os.arch. The order is fixed — SDL3 first, then the JNI bridge — or the dynamic linker binds to a different copy.
guide.platforms.47: Sets POJAV_NATIVEDIR to the APK native dir; loaded by absolute path
guide.platforms.49: No POJAV_NATIVEDIR; the APK native dir sits on LD_LIBRARY_PATH, so System.loadLibrary("SDL3") resolves it
guide.platforms.50: Sets POJAV_NATIVEDIR and loads by absolute path
guide.platforms.51: This is a compatibility note, not a runtime allowlist: any launcher that sets os.version to Android-* takes the Android path, listed or not.
guide.platforms.55: Unsupported — initialization fails and the game still launches, just without a controller
guide.platforms.57: Do not override os.version. Some launchers' custom JVM arguments or version JSON replace it with a plain kernel number (e.g. 5.0) or drop the Android- prefix. The mod then treats the JVM as desktop Linux, loads a desktop SDL3, and the controller never shows up in settings. Make sure the launcher's -Dos.version=Android-<release> is not overridden by your own arguments.
guide.platforms.58: The JAR ships no Android libSDL3.so; do not drop another SDL3 next to your mods. Loading an SDL without the launcher glue makes controllers permanently invisible.
guide.platforms.59: To supply your own libgamepadjni.so, point CFX_LIB_PATH at the directory holding it (system property wins over environment variable).
guide.platforms.60: On Android, SDL is shared with the launcher inside one process, so the mod never SDL_Quits the whole library on shutdown — that would tear down the launcher's video / glue.
guide.platforms.61: The config directory is still config/controlflex/, relative to the game directory the launcher assigned to that instance; switching launchers (or instance dirs) does not carry configs over.
guide.platforms.62: Rumble, cursor, and split-screen availability depends on the launcher's window model and the device: split-screen targets multi-instance desktop setups, and Android devices normally cannot run two instances side by side.

guide.platforms.85: 1 · Hide the on-screen virtual mouse pointer
guide.platforms.86: The pointer the launcher draws is its own overlay and has nothing to do with the mod's virtual cursor — the two do not track each other, so you end up with two pointers on screen, or with one that sits wherever you last touched while the actual click lands somewhere else.
guide.platforms.87: Three equivalent ways to get rid of it; pick whichever your launcher exposes:
guide.platforms.88: turn the pointer display off (hide the virtual mouse cursor)
guide.platforms.90: set the pointer opacity to 0, i.e. fully transparent
guide.platforms.91: After that only the mod's own cursor is on screen and its position matches where clicks land. Style and scale are set in game under Cursor Style: System / Bedrock / Hand, scale 0.1–1.0.
guide.platforms.92: 2 · Set Gamepad Input Mode to SDL Direct (ZL2 / FCL)
guide.platforms.93: In Zalith Launcher 2 and Fold Craft Launcher, Gamepad Input Mode defaults to Mapped (Virtual Keys): buttons and sticks are first translated into virtual keyboard/mouse events, and only then handed to the game. ControlFlex never sees the raw device — no pad in settings, and deadzone, trigger travel, and rumble are all decided by the launcher.
guide.platforms.94: Pick SDL Direct instead. In ZL2 the path is Settings → Gamepad → Gamepad Input Mode, and the option describes itself: raw gamepad input is delivered to the game through the SDL/GLFW gamepad API with button remapping bypassed — exactly what is needed here. SDL3 opens the device directly and the mod reads raw axes and buttons through libgamepadjni, which is the only reason multiple pads, hotplug, and rumble work at all.
guide.platforms.95: Check: in game, Settings → Gamepad Selection lists the device by name and reacts to any button.
guide.platforms.96: Trade-off: once SDL Direct is on, Mapped (Virtual Keys) no longer applies to that pad. That is expected — bind everything in the mod's key mapping panel instead.
guide.platforms.97: Quit the game and relaunch after changing it, so the launcher re-enumerates devices.

compat.bridge.lead: compat JSON can only adjust things that already exist — a registered KeyMapping, a dispatched key, an open screen. If a mod grew its own input system, it has to be wired in on the Java side, and that is a bridge mod. This page answers "do you need code at all" and then gives you a table of the five techniques; the setup steps, the interface details, the five official implementations and the ecosystem list each get their own page.
compat.bridge.decide.h2: First: do you actually need code?
compat.bridge.decide.json.1: Place registered keys on Main / Screen / Overlay
compat.bridge.decide.java.1: Make keys that never registered a KeyMapping appear in the binding list
compat.bridge.decide.json.2: Choose the dispatch channel (including the GLFW polling mirror)
compat.bridge.decide.java.2: Reach mods that call GLFW.glfwGetKey directly (the GLFW layer cannot be injected)
compat.bridge.decide.json.3: Suppress actions by main-hand item plus player state
compat.bridge.decide.java.3: Push the mod's runtime state into Control Flex for use as a condition
compat.bridge.decide.json.4: Phase persistence, ignored keys, tips, per-screen stick parameters
compat.bridge.decide.java.4: Announce that a mod has taken over an overlay or the camera, so stick and look behavior can switch
compat.bridge.decide.json.5: Fall back to virtual keyboard / mouse for mods that only see physical keys
compat.bridge.decide.java.5: Run fully custom logic off the stick axes (vehicle steering, camera), or forward an action into the mod's own function
compat.bridge.decide.rule: One-line test: if the mod's keys show up under Key Mapping → that mod, you do not need a bridge; if they do not, you do. The three tools are cumulative — auto-discovery → compat JSON → bridge; do not skip the first two and start writing code.
compat.bridge.api.1: A separate repository, ControlFlexMC/control-flex-api, published through JitPack; currently 0.9.2 — the same source as 0.9.0, with 0.9.2 being a re-tag for JitPack.
compat.bridge.api.2: The artifact is Java 8 bytecode (class 52), so it loads on any JVM 8+; a bridge mod does not have to share the core mod's toolchain.
compat.bridge.api.3: compileOnly only: Control Flex provides it at runtime. Do not bundle the API into your jar.
compat.bridge.api.4: Scope: read controller input, query action states, push mod states, declare interactive overlays, take over the camera, install compat / guide assets.
compat.bridge.api.callout: The first line is always an availability check — Control Flex may not be installed, and SDL3 may have failed to initialize. Every provider can be null.
compat.bridge.skeleton.col.when: When it runs / what it is for
compat.bridge.skeleton.modid: Plugin identifier, used for logging and de-duplication.
compat.bridge.skeleton.compat: Called before ready; use installer.install() to install compat JSON into compat/mods/.
compat.bridge.skeleton.ready: The single initialization callback; every provider is ready at this point.
compat.bridge.skeleton.conn: Fires when a controller connects or disconnects.
compat.bridge.skeleton.version: Default method that checks the minimum API version and returns false when unmet.
compat.bridge.skeleton.spi: Registration goes through an SPI services file; Control Flex discovers plugins automatically:
compat.bridge.skeleton.layers: Installed JSON lands in compat/mods/: above default/, below user/ — so players can still override your defaults in the user layer, a bridge never locks them out. A same-named file is replaced wholesale; there is no field-level merge.
compat.bridge.official.p: Compatibility work comes in three kinds, all under the ControlFlexMC org: the core mod (built-in JSON + dispatch channels), the config source (distribution of community JSON), and bridges — the 5 that actually write Java.
compat.bridge.official.note: Bridge and JSON are not either/or: most bridges also install a JSON file into the mods/ layer in onInstallCompatConfigs — letting JSON decide where keys go and Java decide what happens at runtime. In the community source the create / emi configs go the other way and use dependencies to require the bridge.
compat.bridge.p1.h3: 1) Keys are not registered at all: add pseudo KeyMappings (EMI)
compat.bridge.p1.p: Register ordinary KeyMappings so auto-discovery sees them, then forward the press into the mod's own entry point — no fake input, no changes to the mod's key settings.
compat.bridge.p2.h3: 2) The mod reads raw key state: mixin into its read point (vehicles / Create)
compat.bridge.p2.p: The glfwPoll channel covers polling through InputConstants.isKeyDown, but mods that call GLFW.glfwGetKey never see it — GLFW is loaded by the system class loader and never passes through ModLauncher's transformer. Instead, put a mixin on the mod's own read entry point and answer "is it held right now".
compat.bridge.p2.note: Keeping that mixin inside a separate bridge mod keeps the core free of third-party dependencies, and a failure only affects that one compat package.
compat.bridge.p3.h3: 3) The mod has runtime state: push a state and let JSON consume it (Epic Fight)
compat.bridge.p3.p: Epic Fight's battle mode decides which keys the mod should own. Java only pushes the state; which actions get suppressed is written in JSON — so players and pack authors can change it.
compat.bridge.ship.1: Log prefix [ModCompat]: config loading, overriding and skip reasons all land there; use your own logger for bridge messages (LogManager.getLogger("my-mod-id")).
compat.bridge.ship.2: Guard the minimum API version with requireApiVersion("0.8.8"), and declare Control Flex as a mandatory dependency in mods.toml / fabric.mod.json.
compat.bridge.ship.3: API is compileOnly; ship a separate JAR and do not shade it in, or you duplicate the core.
compat.bridge.ship.4: Keep the target mod compileOnly too (CurseForge Maven / Modrinth Maven), and add a path that exits quietly when it is missing — that is how the vehicle bridge stays optional.
compat.bridge.skeleton.camera: Return an ICameraLookConsumer to take over each frame's look delta (0.8.8+, see camera takeover); null means no takeover.

compat.bridge.ref.button.note: ButtonName gives three groups: buttons (A…Y, DPAD_UP, LEFT_BUMPER, LEFT_TRIGGER, LEFT_STICK_CLICK, BACK, START, GUIDE, PADDLE_1…PADDLE_4, TOUCHPAD), stick directions (LEFT_STICK_UP …) and axes (AXIS_LEFT_X, AXIS_RIGHT_TRIGGER …).
compat.bridge.ref.registry.note: stateKey is modId:stateName (e.g. epicfight:battle_mode) — exactly the string compat JSON reads in itemSuppressKeys[].playerState.
compat.bridge.ref.camera.1: Why: a mod has taken over the rendered camera (Epic Fight's TPS combat camera, lock-on, …), so the player's yRot/xRot is no longer what you see; the look delta has to be handed to that mod.
compat.bridge.ref.camera.2: Called at most once per frame; the arguments are deltas calibrated before turning, the same scale the vanilla mouse pipeline hands to the mod that took over.
compat.bridge.ref.camera.3: Override cameraLookConsumer() in your plugin and return an implementation; returning null (the default) means no takeover.
compat.bridge.ref.context.note: className is the fully qualified class name — Control Flex looks it up in the compat JSON overlay table to resolve stick and cursor behavior. Null-check first: getInteractiveContextRegistrar() may be null.

compat.bridge.ef.h3: cfx-compat-epicfight: making Control Flex EF's controller backend
compat.bridge.ef.1: Epic Fight does not read KeyMapping; it has its own input SPI (IEpicFightControllerMod). With nothing registered it falls back to raw GLFW keyboard state, which a gamepad binding can never satisfy. It also looks up a ControllerBinding per action, and only the implementor can supply that object — JSON cannot.
compat.bridge.ef.2: So the bridge does three things: implements IEpicFightControllerMod (stick → PlayerInputState, actions → ControllerBinding); mixins over EF's controllerBinding() to redirect binding lookup into Control Flex's action state; listens for ChangePlayerModeEvent and pushes epicfight:battle_mode. On top of that, EpicFightCameraBridge implements camera takeover — turn deltas go to EpicFightCameraAPI.turnCamera(), so the view tracks the stick while EF owns the camera (TPS combat camera, lock-on).
compat.bridge.ef.3: Requires ControlFlex ≥ 0.8.8; Epic Fight ≥ 20.14 (1.20.1 Forge) / ≥ 21.15 (1.21.1 NeoForge). Incompatible with Controlify — both want to be EF's controller mod and only one can win. Source entry points: CfxEpicFightControllerMod, EpicFightStateBridge, EpicFightCameraBridge, mixin/EpicFightInputActionMixin.
compat.bridge.create.h3: cfx-compat-create: one injection point for train throttle
compat.bridge.create.1: Create's train console does not read KeyMapping.isDown(); it walks all the way down to InputConstants.isKeyDown(window, code). Control Flex's analog movement takes over the MOVE group — those actions stop being dispatched and the stick value goes straight into player.input.forwardImpulse — so the player walks, but no key press is ever published and the train never gets throttle.
compat.bridge.create.2: The fix is deliberately minimal: a single RETURN injection on ControlsUtil.isActuallyPressed(KeyMapping) merges forwardImpulse / leftImpulse into the forward / back / left / right checks; sneak → brake, jump → horn. When the real key is already down the original result is returned untouched, so keyboard priority survives.
compat.bridge.create.3: Note it writes no global state: no synthetic GLFW poll state, no KeyMapping writes, no Forge key events, so other mods are unaffected. It needs no "is the player driving?" check either, because only the train console calls isActuallyPressed. Source entry points: CreateTrainControl, mixin/ControlsUtilMixin.
compat.bridge.exposure.1: Exposure's viewfinder is an interactive overlay that grabs the camera and hides the HUD. Control Flex only switches stick behavior for contexts it knows about, so the bridge just reports: mixins on CameraClient.setupViewfinder / removeViewfinder — the two chokepoints every open/close path goes through — call notifyOverlayForeground / notifyOverlayBackground.
compat.bridge.exposure.2: The detail is in pairing: the bridge keeps its own foreground flag, so removeViewfinder without an active viewfinder never emits a stray background; switching cameras emits background → foreground in that order; logging out resets state and emits one final background. Requires ControlFlex ≥ 0.8.7 (0.8.7 renamed these two methods) and Exposure ≥ 1.9.20.
compat.bridge.emi.1: EMI stores its keybinds in its own config (binds.*) and matches them inside its own screens — it registers no Minecraft KeyMapping, so its actions appear neither in vanilla Controls nor in controller auto-discovery. The bridge registers 22 pseudo KeyMappings for Control Flex to discover and forwards each press into EMI's own interaction functions: no fake input, and EMI's key settings are left untouched.
compat.bridge.emi.actions.screen: Toggle EMI, focus search, clear search
compat.bridge.emi.actions.browse: View recipes / uses, add to favourites, recipe tree, stack tree, forward / back
compat.bridge.emi.actions.craft: Craft one / a stack, to inventory (one / stack), to cursor (one)
compat.bridge.emi.actions.creative: Cheat one / a stack to inventory or cursor
compat.bridge.emi.actions.manage: Hide item, hide by ID, copy recipe ID
compat.bridge.emi.2: All of them live in the GUI layer and show up as "Control Flex x EMI" in the binding list. Most act on the hovered stack, so point at the item first; while a text field has focus, or EMI is switched off or reloading, only "Toggle EMI" fires. Not supported: defaultStack, deleteCursorStack, showCraft (the first two are inline logic deep inside the recipe screen, the third is a held state rather than an action), displayAllRecipes (not in the released jar), and "Copy Recipe ID" on a recipe screen (its context sits in a private field). It never rewrites EMI's own binds.* either.
compat.bridge.vehicles.1: Immersive Vehicles (MTS) reads input through GLFW.glfwGetKey(window, keyCode) — it looks at neither KeyMapping nor InputConstants, so keyMapping / virtualKbm / glfwPoll all fail to reach it. The GLFW layer itself is not injectable on Forge (library classes are loaded by the system class loader and never pass through ModLauncher), so the mixin has to sit in the vehicle mod's own read path: InterfaceInputMixin hooks mcinterface1201.InterfaceInput#isKeyPressed and answers true for the four movement keys.
compat.bridge.vehicles.2: The signal is still the player's own forwardImpulse / leftImpulse (including the analog response curve), falling back to action states when they are zero, so it keeps working with analog movement off; nothing is polled, no global key state is written, and a physically pressed key always wins. It ships no JSON: it reads the core mod's signals directly, so there is no rule set to keep in sync with the config format. Known limits: IV's own keybinds (car.gas, …) are ignored, so reset them to WASD if you changed them; do not bind IV's built-in joystick, which sets kbOverride and disables the bridge; the mixin targets a version-stamped package (mcinterface1201), so another MC version needs its own build.
compat.bridge.p4.p: A self-drawn HUD is not a Screen, so Control Flex cannot see it. Report once on open and once on close and the core mod switches stick and cursor behavior in the Overlay phase using the JSON overlay table; the class name must match the overlay key.
compat.bridge.p4.note: Paired notifications are mandatory: foreground without background leaves stick behavior stuck in overlay mode; use clearAll() as the fallback when leaving the world.
compat.bridge.p5.h3: 5) A mod took the camera: consume the look delta
compat.bridge.p5.p: Once the camera is taken over, writing yRot/xRot changes nothing on screen. Implement ICameraLookConsumer and hand the delta to whoever owns the camera; returning true means the frame is consumed and the core mod will not write player rotation.
compat.bridge.ship.5: Multi-loader projects use three modules, common/ + forge/ + fabric/: logic in common, mixin config and mod metadata per loader.
compat.bridge.ship.6: When you publish, state what it fixes, which mod versions and loaders you tested, whether it ships optional JSON defaults, and which mods it conflicts with.

compat.bridge.layout.p: All five official bridges use the same three-module layout: the logic is written once in common/, and the loader-specific parts (mixin config, mod metadata, event bus) stay in forge/ and fabric/. Adding an MC version line then only touches metadata instead of copying the logic.
compat.bridge.layout.note: Two easy traps. First, the SPI service file has to live in common's resources/META-INF/services — keep it only in a loader module and Fabric will never see it. Second, either keep the target mod strictly compileOnly or write an explicit "target missing, exit quietly" branch, otherwise your bridge drags the whole game down with it.
compat.bridge.err.1.cause: Wrong SPI path or class name, or getPluginId() returns an empty string and is dropped as a duplicate. Check the discovery pass in the [ModCompat] log.
compat.bridge.err.2.cause: Control Flex registers its providers in stages; only after ready is everything available. In the earlier callbacks, stick to installing assets.
compat.bridge.err.3.sym: JSON installed but the keys never appear
compat.bridge.err.3.cause: The file must sit in compat/mods/ and be named after the mod_id; a mod_versions[].version that does not match the installed mod version is skipped as well.
compat.bridge.err.4.cause: Mixin configs must be declared in xxx.mixins.json and listed in fabric.mod.json's mixins field; NeoForge 1.20.5+ uses META-INF/neoforge.mods.toml.
compat.bridge.err.5.cause: Only one gamepad backend may drive a given target mod. The Epic Fight bridge is mutually exclusive with Controlify — say so in your release notes.

compat.overview.lead: Control Flex is built for mid-to-large modpacks: zero configuration by default, escalating only when a mod's input refuses to behave. This page maps out what each of the five tools can do, when to climb to the next one, and where the result ends up.
compat.overview.ladder.p: From zero cost to writing code — a ladder you only climb when the rung below does not work. Each step down is more precise, and more expensive to maintain.
compat.overview.ladder.r1.covers: Mods that register their keys through KeyMapping
compat.overview.ladder.r2.need: A controller and a few minutes
compat.overview.ladder.r2.covers: Key layering, plus stick and cursor behavior for screens and overlays
compat.overview.ladder.r3.need: A network connection, or a ready-made file
compat.overview.ladder.r3.covers: The shareable form of the two rungs above, plus dispatch channels, key suppression and tips
compat.overview.ladder.r4.need: A text editor and the field reference
compat.overview.ladder.r4.covers: Fine-grained rules: per-key channels, item suppression, phase persistence, per-screen stick parameters
compat.overview.ladder.r5.covers: Input systems that bypass KeyMapping, runtime state, custom-drawn UIs
compat.overview.ladder.note: Most modpacks stop at rungs 1–3. Only a handful of mods genuinely need a bridge — usually the ones that ship their own input system: EMI, Create's train console, Immersive Vehicles, Epic Fight.
compat.overview.escalate.1: First check Key Mapping for it — if the key is there, it is a standard KeyMapping mod and rungs 2 / 3 will do.
compat.overview.escalate.2: The key exists but nothing happens in a screen — usually the wrong phase or the wrong dispatch path: add a screen / overlay rule on rung 2, then change the channel on rung 3.
compat.overview.escalate.3: Nothing on press, or the action fires twice — the dispatch channel is wrong (eventBus and keyMapping both firing). Pin it down on rung 4.
compat.overview.escalate.4: The key never shows up at all — the mod keeps bindings in its own config, polls raw key state, or reads the gamepad directly. Only rung 5 can reach it.
compat.overview.escalate.5: The mod has runtime state such as a battle mode — the bridge pushes the state (IPlayerStateRegistry) and JSON consumes it through itemSuppressKeys' playerState condition.
compat.overview.model.h2: 3. One data model underneath all five
compat.overview.model.p: Whichever rung you use, what lands on disk is the same compat JSON. The core is three key sections plus one dispatch concept:
compat.overview.model.inGame.use: Combat keys, skill keys, transformation keys
compat.overview.model.overlay.when: An overlay is open (wheels or circles drawn over the HUD)
compat.overview.model.overlay.use: Spell wheels, radial menus, photo HUDs
compat.overview.model.channels: How a press reaches the mod is decided by the dispatch channel: keyMapping, eventBus, glfwPoll, screenInput, virtualKbm. Different keys in the same file can use different channels — which is also the fix for double-firing keys.
compat.overview.layers.h2: 4. Where the result lives: three layers
compat.overview.layers.p: Compat configs load from three layers, priority user > mods > default; the same mod_id is replaced wholesale, never merged field by field. Which layer to edit — and what can overwrite it — is covered in Editing configs by hand.

compat.json.lead: Compat JSON is the shareable unit behind the whole system: the in-game UI writes it, the community repo distributes it, bridge mods install it. This page covers where files go, how the fields work, how to contribute a config, and how to run your own source.
compat.json.files.h2: 1. Where files go, and when they load
compat.json.files.1: Three directories: compat/default/ (extracted from the JAR, read-only), compat/mods/ (installed by bridge mods, read-only), compat/user/ (your changes, highest priority).
compat.json.files.2: Identity comes from the mod_id inside the JSON, not the filename — but files in user/ must be named <mod_id>.json, because the UI and hot-reload look them up by that name.
compat.json.files.3: Three gates must all pass: the target mod_id is installed, every mod listed in dependencies is loaded, and one entry in mod_versions matches the installed mod version. If any fails, the whole file is skipped (the log distinguishes "mod not loaded" from "dependencies not loaded").
compat.json.files.4: Files starting with a dot (such as .applied.json) are never parsed as configs.
compat.json.files.5: Legacy {modid}_keys.json files are migrated automatically on startup: the original is backed up and renamed, the fields converted.
compat.json.builtin.p: Only three configs are bundled, extracted to config/controlflex/compat/default/ on every launch:
compat.json.builtin.jei: Recipe / uses keys placed on the screen layer, plus a batch of internal keys added to ignoreKeys
compat.json.builtin.epicfight: Battle-mode keys and screen rules, pointing at the official bridge cfx-compat-epicfight
compat.json.builtin.nightfall: Key and screen adaptation for the mod
compat.json.builtin.note: exempt_mods.json in the same directory is not a compat config — it declares library mods (Fabric API, Kotlin language support and friends) so they never clutter the adaptation lists. Everything else is covered by auto-discovery or the community repo.
compat.json.repo.p1: The official source is ControlFlexMC/cfx-compat-configs: a purely static directory tree, split by MC version and loader, one JSON per mod, plus a manifest.json recording each path and sha256.
compat.json.repo.p2: The client requests exactly two kinds of URL: {baseUrl}/{mcVersion}/{loader}/manifest.json and the content files referenced by path in that manifest. Only the current loader's directory is read; a missing version / loader is a 404 — normal, not a failure, and it does not affect other sources.
compat.json.repo.p3: In game: Settings → Mod Adaptation → “More” (top right) → Sync latest configs. The mod's detail page then shows a “N community adaptation configs found” banner → pick a variant → read-only preview → Apply. Apply backs up the old user file, overwrites atomically, records it in .applied.json, and hot-reloads that mod — no restart.
compat.json.repo.p4: Same mod_id with different content = parallel variants for the player to choose from; the same sha256 in several sources = mirrors, retried in source-list order. Content is cached by sha256 at compat/repo/content/<mod_id>/<sha256>.json; those files are immutable.
compat.json.top.mod_id: The mod ID this config belongs to (e.g. jei, epicfight). Empty, or the mod not installed → the whole file is skipped; it is part of the activation gate itself.
compat.json.top.dependencies: Extra gate: { "mod_id": "...", "mod_name": "...", "home_pages": [...] }. Only mod_id is read at runtime; all of them must be loaded for the config to activate.
compat.json.top.contributors: Author names, shown on the community-config preview page.
compat.json.top.config_version: Version of this config itself — display only, no runtime logic.
compat.json.top.mod_versions: Version-specific rule sets, see below. The legacy name versions is no longer accepted.
compat.json.top.meta: Pure metadata for the manifest generator and the preview UI; ignored at runtime.
compat.json.mv.p: The array is evaluated in order and the first match wins; if nothing matches the installed mod version, the entire config has no effect (a warning is logged).
compat.json.mv.1: Comparison is numeric per dot-separated segment: missing segments count as 0, non-digit prefixes are stripped (v1.0 → 1.0, 0-beta → 0).
compat.json.mv.2: A malformed interval (missing bracket / comma, unparseable bound, lower > upper) discards the whole entry, not just the field.
compat.json.mv.3: Put specific intervals first and finish with a "" wildcard as fallback.
compat.json.sections.h3: The three sections and dispatch channels
compat.json.sections.p: All three sections are objects mapping a bare key name to per-key settings. A bare key name is KeyMapping.getName() without the modid: prefix; the action ID is still {modid}:{keyName}. A key listed in several sections belongs to all of them (union); a key declared in none defaults to in-game only.
compat.json.ch.keyMapping: Writes KeyMapping.setPressed() / isDown state — the same path vanilla uses.
compat.json.ch.glfwPoll: Mirrors the hold into synthetic InputConstants.isKeyDown() state, for mods that poll GLFW themselves.
compat.json.ch.screenInput: While a screen is open, feeds screen.keyPressed/keyReleased (or a synthetic click for mouse-bound keys).
compat.json.ch.virtualKbm: Injected through the virtual keyboard / mouse as real hardware input. Exclusive: replaces every other channel and is not user-overridable.
compat.json.ch.defaults.p: Defaults when a section declares no channels:
compat.json.ch.fix1: The mod fires twice (listening on both paths) → keep only keyMapping.
compat.json.ch.fix2: The mod only listens to Forge events → ["eventBus"].
compat.json.ch.fix3: A hold-to-open menu that polls GLFW itself → add glfwPoll.
compat.json.extra.p: Per-key behavior flags; there is one value today: suppressLayerSwitch — while that action's binding is held, layer switching is suppressed, and the binding is forced to HOLD on save. Use it for modded modifier-style keys (Iron's Spells' key.irons_spellbooks.spell_bar_modifier, for example). An explicit [] means explicitly off.
compat.json.phase.p: Declares that a key's binding should follow it across a phase switch:
compat.json.phase.1: Only ["inGame", "overlay"] and ["inGame", "screen"] are allowed: the source must be inGame and exactly one destination.
compat.json.phase.2: The key must also be declared in both sections; the pairing alone is ignored (and warned about) — implicit membership via the union does not count.
compat.json.phase.3: At runtime the destination layer's binding is soft-locked and derived live from the game layers (no copy is persisted): a held button stays held across the transition, so a hold-to-open menu does not flicker shut when a screen or overlay appears.
compat.json.phase.4: These bindings are materialized as HOLD and skip item suppression. Editing the destination layer in the binding UI writes a snapshot binding and unlocks it; resetting the key restores the lock and the derivation.
compat.json.ignore.p: Hides actions from the binding UI (debug keys, cheat keys, duplicates): "ignoreKeys": ["key.epicfight.config"]. The modid: prefix is added automatically when matching action IDs.
compat.json.suppress.p: Suppresses actions while the main-hand item matches. Typical case: the mod takes over input for specific items (in battle mode, attack / interact are handled by the mod's combo and weapon-skill systems), so the generic actions are suppressed to stop them fighting each other.
compat.json.suppress.item: Item ID (modid:item_id); * wildcard supported. Mutually exclusive with tag.
compat.json.suppress.state: Optional modId:state list (OR); empty = suppress whenever the item matches. Unknown states warn and count as no-match.
compat.json.suppress.actions: Action short names (attack, use) or full action IDs.
compat.json.suppress.note: Evaluated once per tick against the main-hand item; actions matched by phasePersistentKeys are exempt.
compat.json.tips.p: Hint text shown on binding rows:
compat.json.tips.note: Language codes have no whitelist: the runtime uses the player's language and falls back to en_us; with no en_us nothing is shown. Always include en_us.
compat.json.screen.h3: Stick and cursor behavior per screen / overlay
compat.json.screen.p: Keys are fully qualified class names: screen.getClass().getName() for screens; the opener class name for overlays, with "*" as the mod-level fallback.
compat.json.screen.default: Engine default: incremental virtual mouse on the left stick, nothing on the right stick in a GUI
compat.json.screen.mouse: The stick drives the incremental virtual cursor
compat.json.screen.radial: Polar cursor from the screen center (wheel-style UIs)
compat.json.screen.disabled: The axis is ignored; stick-click bindings still work
compat.json.screen.radius: Distance from the screen center (logical pixels × GUI scale)
compat.json.screen.show: Whether to draw the cursor (false still tracks position, just does not draw it)
compat.json.screen.keep: Stay in place when the stick is released
compat.json.screen.note: Entries also accept cursorStyle (system / bedrock / hand) and disabled: true (opt out entirely, no fallback). Resolution: user layer before built-ins, a specific overlay entry before the same mod's "*", and a hit that lacks the requested side (left / right) falls through to the next config.
compat.json.min.callout: The above is the quick-reference version. The complete field set, the real behavior of each channel, and the migration table from the ≤ 0.8.5 format live in the authoritative reference: English / Chinese.
compat.json.contribute.1: Fork the repo and switch to the matching branch. The config format changes between ControlFlex versions and sources are consumed per branch; if your fork only has the default branch, pull the version branch down first.
compat.json.contribute.2: Create <mc-version>/<loader>/mods/<mod_id>.json. Use the bare key names from the mod's Controls category (no modid: prefix); the [ModCompat] log lines help you find them.
compat.json.contribute.3: Regenerate the manifest: python3 generate_manifest.py. Editing content without recomputing sha256 is the number one cause of "content download failed" on the player side.
compat.json.contribute.4: Verify in game. Add your fork as a source, or drop the file into compat/user/ and restart. Check the [ModCompat] log to confirm it loaded.
compat.json.contribute.5: Open a PR stating the mod version tested, the loader(s), and what the config fixes.
compat.json.contribute.note: If a config only matters on one loader, keep it in that loader's directory; if it behaves the same everywhere, copy the file into the other directories. Files are capped at 2 MB (real configs are a few KB).
compat.json.source.p: A "source" is just a static HTTP directory tree: {baseUrl}/{mcVersion}/{loader}/manifest.json plus content files. No server-side logic, so any static host will do.
compat.json.source.route.fork: Fork the official repo (recommended): the layout, the manifest generator and a set of working configs are already there — you only add your own. The cost is keeping up with upstream.
compat.json.source.route.scratch: Build a tree from scratch: your own release cadence, private or experimental configs — just follow the layout below.
compat.json.source.schema: Number; greater than 1 is rejected (the client shows an upgrade hint); missing or 0 is tolerated.
compat.json.source.mod_id: Must match ^[a-z0-9_-]+$ and be unique within the manifest; a duplicate fails the entire manifest parse.
compat.json.source.path: Relative to the manifest's directory; absolute paths, backslashes, empty segments and .. are rejected. The convention is mods/<file>.json.
compat.json.source.sha: SHA-256 of the content file, 64 lowercase hex characters. Verified after download; a mismatch tries the next mirror. It is the sole identity of a variant.
compat.json.source.meta: Display-only fields (dependencies is for display; the client never installs dependencies).
compat.json.source.manifest.note: The official repo's generate_manifest.py can be reused as is: it scans <mc-version>/<loader>/mods/*.json, extracts mod_id / mod_name / home_page, computes the sha256 and writes the manifest back idempotently.
compat.json.source.cache.raw: About 5 minutes; the official built-in sources use this form
compat.json.source.cache.cdn: Branch refs cache for roughly 12 hours; prefer a tag
compat.json.source.limit.url: Must be http:// or https:// with a host name
compat.json.source.limit.redirect.v: 301/302/303/307/308 followed, max 5 hops; https → http downgrades rejected
compat.json.source.add.1: Go to Settings → Mod Adaptation → “More” (top right) → Edit source list.
compat.json.source.add.2: Paste the baseUrl into the input at the bottom → Add → Done; closing the dialog with a changed list triggers a background sync.
compat.json.source.add.3: Open “Sync latest configs” and confirm your source synced (per-source progress and logs); the mod cards then show a community-config badge.
compat.json.source.add.note: Source-list behavior: built-ins can be disabled and reordered but not deleted; your own sources can be added, removed and reordered freely; “Restore default sources” only resets the two built-ins. Each source caches under compat/repo/manifest/<source-id>/, where the id is derived from the URL (lowercase, with -1 / -2 on conflicts).
compat.json.source.local.note: http:// sources are allowed (only https → http redirect downgrades are rejected), so local testing needs no certificate. Edit files, then hit “Sync latest configs” once.
compat.json.troubleshoot.1.c: Open {baseUrl}/{mcVersion}/{loader}/manifest.json in a browser; directory names must exactly match the game version name and loader name (1.20.1, not 1.20).
compat.json.troubleshoot.2.c: Duplicate mod_id, path with an absolute path / backslash / .., sha256 that is not 64 lowercase hex characters, schemaVersion > 1, or a JSON syntax error.
compat.json.troubleshoot.3.s: Manifest synced but content download fails
compat.json.troubleshoot.3.c: The content bytes do not match the manifest sha256 (edited the JSON but forgot to regenerate the manifest is the usual cause), the file exceeds 2 MB, or every mirror failed in that round.
compat.json.troubleshoot.4.c: The config's own gates failed: the mod_id mod is missing, dependencies are not all loaded, no mod_versions entry matches (first match wins — mind interval syntax and order), or a key name is wrong. Search the [ModCompat] log.
compat.json.troubleshoot.5.c: jsDelivr caches @branch for about 12 hours; switch to the raw URL, cut a tag, or wait for the cache to expire.
compat.json.troubleshoot.6.c: The file must be UTF-8 (BOM-free preferred).
compat.json.pin.h3: How the official source pins versions
compat.json.pin.1: Two built-in sources point at the same ref: cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ControlFlexMC/cfx-compat-configs@<ref> and raw.githubusercontent.com/ControlFlexMC/cfx-compat-configs/refs/heads/<ref>. The first is fast, the second is dependable; they mirror each other.
compat.json.pin.2: <ref> is a version tag (currently 0.8.8), bumped with every ControlFlex release — not main — so players on older builds always sync configs their format can read and never get broken by an upstream format change.
compat.json.pin.3: That is why the repo keeps one branch / tag per version line: 0.8.4, 0.8.5, 0.8.7, 0.8.8… To backfill configs for an old version, switch to that branch instead of dropping old-format files on main.
compat.json.pin.4: The two built-in sources can be disabled and reordered but not deleted; "Restore default sources" only resets those two. Your own sources can be added and removed freely.
compat.json.cover.p: Directories are split by MC version / loader, and 12 mods have configs so far. The same config is usually copied into every loader directory it applies to, so coverage differs between version lines:
compat.json.cover.note: This table follows the repo; the directory tree is authoritative. The create / emi configs also require their bridge mod through dependencies — the keys come from the bridge.
compat.json.deps.p: It is not "install dependencies for you" but an activation gate: the config only applies when every mod_id in the array is loaded. Real configs use it in two situations — the config depends on keys a bridge mod provides, or the config belongs to a standalone compat mod.
compat.json.deps.note: Only mod_id is read (case-insensitive); mod_name / home_pages are display-only on the community preview page. An array of plain strings, or a non-array value, is ignored wholesale. A config whose target is the mod itself does not need it.
compat.json.legacy.p: Since 0.8.7 old files are migrated automatically on startup (backed up, then rewritten). If you maintain configs by hand, or have to read an old one, use this table:
compat.json.legacy.row.loader.new: Removed; the source directory (forge / fabric / neoforge) separates loaders
compat.json.legacy.row.persist.new: declared once in the game section and once in the destination section
compat.json.legacy.row.skip.new: screen object keyed by class name + behavior; RADIAL_CURSOR → RADIAL_PATH, returnToCenter: false → keepLastPosition: true
compat.json.legacy.row.new.val: per-overlay overlay config · phase persistence with an overlay destination
compat.json.check.h3: Self-check before you ship a config
compat.json.check.1: The three sections must be objects; the array form is dropped wholesale, with a single warning.
compat.json.check.2: channels inside a section is a reserved key (section defaults) — never use it as a key name.
compat.json.check.3: Per-key channels: [] and extraBehaviors: [] are meaningful explicit empties, not the same as omitting the field.
compat.json.check.4: mod_versions is first-match-wins: specific intervals first, a "" fallback last; no matching entry means the whole config is inert.
compat.json.check.5: A malformed version discards the whole entry, not just the field.
compat.json.check.6: Identity comes from the JSON's mod_id, but user-layer files must be named <mod_id>.json.
compat.json.check.7: phasePersistentKeys only works when the key is declared in both sections; the pairing alone is ignored.
compat.json.check.8: UTF-8, no trailing commas; add channels overrides only when the default behavior misbehaves.
compat.manual.lead: Everything you can tune in game lives in the UI, but sometimes you need a text editor: bulk changes, copying a snippet from someone else's config, repairing a stale one. This page covers which layer to edit, how to do it, and how to undo it.
compat.manual.which.h2: 1. Work out which layer you are editing
compat.manual.which.default.fate: Overwritten on mod upgrade — do not edit this one
compat.manual.which.mods.fate: Overwritten when the bridge updates; also read-only
compat.manual.which.user.who: The in-game UI, Apply, or you
compat.manual.which.user.fate: Highest priority, never overwritten (Apply backs it up first)
compat.manual.which.callout: Overriding is a whole-file replacement, not a field merge: for a given mod_id, a user file replaces both mods/ and default/ entirely. So when you copy a snippet, copy the whole mod_versions block with it.
compat.manual.ui.1: Go to Settings → Mod Adaptation, pick the mod, switch to Key Bindings / Screen Adaptation / Overlay Adaptation.
compat.manual.ui.2: Save — changes are written to compat/user/<mod_id>.json and that mod is hot-reloaded immediately, no restart.
compat.manual.ui.3: If you break something, hit Reset Config: the mod returns to its built-in or applied community default (equivalent to deleting the user file).
compat.manual.ui.note: Rule editing is always copy-on-write: built-in and community files stay read-only and the UI only writes to the user layer. That is why you can never break a built-in config.
compat.manual.file.1: Copy compat/default/<mod_id>.json, or an applied community file — do not start from scratch, it is easy to miss fields.
compat.manual.file.2: Rename it <mod_id>.json and drop it into config/controlflex/compat/user/. The name has to match; both the UI and hot-reload look it up by that name.
compat.manual.file.3: Change only the fields you care about; delete whole entries for keys you do not need. This file applies as a whole, not as a patch.
compat.manual.file.4: Save as UTF-8, and watch out for trailing commas.
compat.manual.file.5: Restart the game to apply. There is no watcher on disk files; only Apply and the in-game editor hot-reload.
compat.manual.file.callout: Broken JSON will not crash the game: the whole file is skipped and a parse error is logged. So check the log after editing instead of blaming the controller.
compat.manual.copy.h2: 4. Option three: take a file straight from a source
compat.manual.copy.p: You do not have to press Sync in game: find <mc-version>/<loader>/mods/<mod_id>.json in cfx-compat-configs, download it into compat/user/ and restart. Handy for pre-seeding a pack or for machines with no network.
compat.manual.copy.note: This does not write .applied.json, so the in-game variant list will not show it as applied — but the config itself works normally.
compat.manual.pitfalls.1: First match wins; a broad interval placed early swallows every later version. Always put the "" wildcard last.
compat.manual.pitfalls.2: Malformed (missing bracket / comma, lower > upper) → the whole entry is discarded, not just that field.
compat.manual.pitfalls.3: The old array form is dropped wholesale, with a warning.
compat.manual.pitfalls.4: It is a reserved key meaning "default channels for this section", never a key name.
compat.manual.pitfalls.5: An explicit empty array is meaningful: this key dispatches nothing — quite different from omitting the field.
compat.manual.pitfalls.6: The key must be declared in both sections; the pairing alone is ignored (and warned about).
compat.manual.pitfalls.7: It must be an installed mod's ID; if the mod is epicfight, writing epic_fight means it never activates.
compat.manual.pitfalls.8: UTF-8, no trailing commas; on Windows, make sure Notepad does not save UTF-16 — tips turn into mojibake immediately.
compat.manual.revert.1: Reset Config in game → back to the built-in or applied community default.
compat.manual.revert.2: Delete compat/user/<mod_id>.json → it falls back to mods/ or default/ automatically.
compat.manual.revert.3: The pre-Apply file is kept at compat/backup/<mod_id>-<yyyyMMdd-HHmmss>.json (repeats within the same second get -1, -2).
compat.manual.revert.4: Applied records live in compat/user/.applied.json; the leading dot keeps it from being parsed as a config.
compat.manual.revert.note: After a rollback, glance at the log to confirm which file is now in effect — especially if you had the same config in several layers.
compat.manual.pack.h2: 7. Shipping the change in a modpack
compat.manual.pack.p: Put compat/user/*.json together with profiles/ into the pack's overrides (on CurseForge / Modrinth, overrides/config/controlflex/). Player changes still land in the user layer and win over your preset files; but remember whole-file semantics — as soon as a player edits the same mod_id, your preset no longer participates.
compat.manual.pack.note: After a mod update, mod_versions may no longer match and the config goes quietly inert. Before releasing, run the new mod version and confirm in the log that the config actually loaded.
